1338.title: Kunti
1338.hook: her sons finally rule, and Kunti walks out of the city toward the forest, with blind Gandhari's hand on her shoulder
1338.howItsDone: Hindus meet Kunti's departure in fuller retellings of the Mahabharata's later books; the ideal of leaving household life for the forest in old age, vanaprastha, is an old stage of life described in Hindu texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kunti sent her sons the story of Vidula: better to blaze for a moment than to smolder for a long time.

A small procession leaves Hastinapura through the gate. In it walks an old blind king, Dhritarashtra, whose sons died in the war. His hand rests on the shoulder of his wife, Gandhari, her eyes bound with cloth. And Gandhari's hand rests on the shoulder of the woman leading them both: Kunti. The Pandavas are on the throne at last. Their mother has everything the war was fought for, and she is walking away from it, into the forest, guiding the parents of the men her sons killed. Her sons run after her. Today: Kunti's last word to them.
screen: `A PROCESSION LEAVES THE CITY.` → `A HAND ON EACH SHOULDER.` → `KUNTI LEADS THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Mahabharata's Book of the Hermitage. Dhritarashtra has decided to end his days in the forest, and Gandhari goes with him. Kunti's sons assume their mother will stay. She doesn't. Yudhishthira begs her. Bhima puts the hard question into words, in paraphrase: you roused us to fight, and now that the kingdom is ours, you leave it? Kunti's answer is the center of the scene. I urged you on, she says, so that you wouldn't live on in humiliation, so that Draupadi would not be wronged again, so that the family's name would stand. Not so that I could enjoy a kingdom. I had my time as a queen, with your father. Now I will serve my husband's elder brother and his wife in the forest. Go back. So the woman who urged the war wanted none of its prize for herself. Then look at who she walks with. Gandhari lost her sons in the war Kunti's sons won, and Kunti chooses to be her guide, her hand under Gandhari's. The epic doesn't explain it with a speech; it just shows the two mothers walking together. And it's a picture of a life with seasons: a time to rule, a time to fight, and now a time to let go, and Kunti seems to know which is which. Tomorrow, the woman with her hand on Kunti's shoulder gets her own days.

Notice whether they're easy or hard to walk with, remembering that Kunti led a woman whose grief her own sons had caused, and stay with the feeling of the hand for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer.

1339.title: Gandhari
1339.hook: her son comes to her for a blessing before battle, and Gandhari will not say the words he wants
1339.howItsDone: Hindus hear Gandhari's words in retellings of the Mahabharata, and some Hindus still quote the phrase yato dharmas tato jayah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kunti walked out of the city with the kingdom won, guiding Gandhari, whose hand rested on her shoulder.

A mother's blessing, before a fight, is supposed to be easy. Go well. Come home. Win. During the war, the Mahabharata says, Duryodhana came to his mother Gandhari and asked for her blessing for victory. He was her son. He was fighting for his life and his crown. All she had to say was, may you win. She never said it. Today Gandhari gets her own days, starting with the words she gave him instead.
screen: `A SON ASKS FOR A BLESSING.` → `MAY YOU WIN.` → `SHE NEVER SAID IT.`

segments.voice: Her answer is a short line in Sanskrit: yato dharmas tato jayah. Where dharma is, there is victory. It's a blessing that refuses to take sides by name. If Duryodhana is in the right, it's a blessing. If he isn't, it's a warning. Gandhari doesn't tell him which; she lets the line do its work. And it wasn't the first time she said hard things to him. Before the war, in the Book of Effort, she is called into the royal court while Krishna's peace mission is failing. She speaks to her son in front of everyone, in paraphrase: a person who can't rule his own senses can't rule a kingdom for long. Make peace with your cousins. She speaks hard words to her husband too, for letting their son go so far. Duryodhana walks out of the hall. Put the two scenes together. It's a mother's love with a spine: she doesn't stop being his mother; she stops flattering him. It's honest about limits: she can't make him listen, only refuse to say what isn't true. And the line outlives the story. After the war, when grief makes her want to curse the victors, the epic reminds her of her own words: where dharma is, there is victory. The answer she gave her son at the hardest hour comes back to steady her own hand.
screen: `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY` · `A BLESSING THAT NAMES NO SIDE` · `SHE WARNS HIM IN OPEN COURT` · `HER OWN WORDS COME BACK TO HER`

1340.title: Gandhari
1340.hook: a folded cloth, tied once over a young bride's eyes, and the many ways people have read it since
1340.howItsDone: Hindus meet Gandhari's blindfold in retellings of the Mahabharata, on stage and screen and in story, where it is held up as an image of a wife's devotion and, in some modern retellings, questioned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhari's answer to her son before battle: where dharma is, there is victory.

Paintings show it. So do films and television. A strip of cloth, tied over Gandhari's eyes. Last year on this path, the story of how it got there was told in passing: a princess of Gandhara learns that the prince she will marry, Dhritarashtra, is blind, and she binds her own eyes. The Mahabharata tells it in a few lines and moves on. Readers have kept coming back to it. Today: Gandhari's blindfold, and the different things people see in it.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `A FEW LINES IN THE EPIC.` → `WHAT PEOPLE SEE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's what the first book of the Mahabharata gives, in paraphrase. Gandhari hears that her husband-to-be is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it over, and binds her eyes, resolving not to go beyond her husband. That's it. No speech. No explanation beyond that one resolve. Readers have filled the silence in different ways. Devotional retellings hear devotion: a wife who would not see what her husband could not, and the strength the stories give her for it. Others hear solidarity, sharing his darkness rather than looking down on it. And some modern readers hear something more troubled: a woman of clear sight who chose not to look, at a court that badly needed someone to look. Those readings sit side by side; the epic doesn't settle them. There's also a story from later retellings. Before his last fight, Gandhari asks Duryodhana to come to her unclothed, so that one look from her long-covered eyes can make his body hard as diamond. He comes, but out of shame covers his waist, and that is where he is struck. It's a story about the power people sensed behind the cloth. A choice made once can shape a whole life. A sacrifice can be read many ways at once, and the person making it doesn't control the reading. And the cloth isn't the end of Gandhari's sight. In the war's aftermath she will see in other ways, and that is tomorrow's story.

segments.voice: If you're somewhere safe, close your eyes or rest a hand gently over them, and notice how the room changes: the sounds come closer, the body gets louder. If you pray, you can ask to see clearly.

1341.title: Gandhari
1341.hook: in the forest, years after the war, Gandhari asks to see her sons once more, and for one night the river gives back the dead
1341.howItsDone: Hindus meet this scene in fuller retellings of the Mahabharata's later books; offerings for the dead, made with water at a river such as the Ganga, remain part of Hindu funeral and memorial rites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhari's blindfold: one folded cloth, read as devotion, solidarity and a refusal to look.

Night on the bank of the Ganga. An old blind king, his wife with her eyes bound, and Kunti beside them sit in the dark with the Pandavas and the widows of the war, waiting. The sage Vyasa has told them to bathe and wait. They are waiting for the dead. It began with Gandhari. In the forest, the Mahabharata says, when Vyasa came to visit, she spoke to him of her grief, and asked whether her sons, and the sons of all those mothers, could be seen once more. Today, the last of Gandhari's days: the night the river gave them back.
screen: `NIGHT ON THE GANGA'S BANK.` → `WAITING FOR THE DEAD.` → `IT BEGAN WITH GANDHARI'S REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Book of the Hermitage, here in paraphrase. When night comes, Vyasa goes into the river and calls the fallen warriors by name. And they rise out of the water, warriors of both sides, in their armor and with their banners, as they looked in life. The text is careful about one thing: they come without anger. The enemies of the battlefield have no quarrel now. Fathers meet sons, wives meet husbands. Kunti sees Karna, the son she acknowledged only after his death. And Gandhari, for this one night, sees her sons. At dawn, the warriors go back into the river, each to the world he has earned, and the living are left on the bank. Look at who asked: Gandhari, who once cursed in her grief, asks this time for something gentler, only to see. Look at what the dead bring: not blame, but a peace with each other that the living had not managed. And it isn't forever. One night, then dawn. The epic doesn't pretend grief can be undone, only that it can be met. Later, the story says, a forest fire comes, and the old king, Gandhari and Kunti meet it sitting still, and are gone together. Gandhari's days end with two mothers who walked into the forest side by side.
screen: `VYASA CALLS THE WARRIORS BY NAME` · `THEY RISE WITHOUT ANGER` · `GANDHARI SEES HER SONS` · `AT DAWN, BACK INTO THE RIVER`

segments.voice: If there's someone you've lost, let them come to mind gently, as they looked when they were well; if no one comes, just sit by the water, and let any old quarrel rest for these breaths, the way the dead in the story came without anger. When you're ready, let them go back, the way the warriors returned at dawn, and if you pray, you can commend them to God's keeping. If grief ever feels like more than you can carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

1342.title: Savitri
1342.hook: a childless king keeps offering with one verse, and the daughter he is given carries its name
1342.howItsDone: Hindus who keep the daily twilight rite, sandhya, recite the Gayatri, also called the Savitri, at dawn and dusk; Savitri's story itself is retold at home and in temple talks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhari by the Ganga: she asked only to see her sons, and for one night the dead rose without anger.

A verse with a second name. Earlier this year, the verse to the sun that people call the Gayatri turned up in the older law books as the Savitri, the verse to the god Savitr. Keep that name in your pocket. In the Mahabharata, a sage sitting with the exiled Pandavas in the forest tells of a king with no child, and the verse he keeps offering with is that one. Last year we heard Savitri's whole story. This time we stay with the woman herself, starting where she starts: with her name.
screen: `THE GAYATRI HAS A SECOND NAME.` → `A KING WITH NO CHILD.` → `WHERE HER NAME CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: The king is Ashvapati, ruler of the Madras. The epic calls him good, truthful and generous, and grieved by one thing: there is no child in his house. So he takes up a discipline. He eats sparingly and keeps his senses in check. Again and again, into the sacred fire, he makes offerings with the Savitri verse, and he keeps it up a long time. Then one day the fire answers. The goddess Savitri herself rises out of it, pleased with him, and offers him a gift. He asks for children. She tells him a daughter will be born to him, full of radiance. When the girl comes, the king names her after the goddess who gave her: Savitri. A name that belonged to a verse, then to a goddess, now belongs to a baby. Think about what the verse asks for. In paraphrase: may the sun god stir our thoughts. And the girl named for it grows into a woman who keeps her thinking clear under pressure. She goes out and chooses. She hears a terrible warning and doesn't flinch. She will stand in front of Death and keep talking. The epic doesn't spell out that link. It gives her the name and lets her grow into it. One more turn. The law books hang this verse on the edges of the day, dawn and dusk, said while the light is changing. Savitri's whole story happens at an edge like that, between a life and its end: a verse for the turning of the light, made into a woman who stands in the turning and keeps her head.

1343.title: Savitri
1343.hook: the warning was spoken at her father's court, and in the forest, only Savitri carries it
1343.howItsDone: Hindus hear Savitri's story in the Mahabharata's forest book, where the sage Markandeya tells it to Yudhishthira; it is retold in homes and temples, often around the vow some married women keep in her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri's name: a verse to the sun, a goddess who rose from her father's fire, and a baby named for both.

The warning was spoken once, in a palace. When the sage Narada said that Satyavan would die within the year, he said it at a royal court, to Savitri and her father. Then the wedding happened in a forest hermitage, far from that court. Satyavan didn't hear the warning. His parents didn't. The hermits didn't. So Savitri moves into her new home carrying a sentence about her husband that nobody around her has heard. Today: what she does with it, and what she doesn't say.
screen: `WHO ELSE KNEW?` → `THE WARNING STAYED AT COURT.` → `SHE CARRIES IT ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, what she does. She takes off her jewels and wears the rough cloth of the forest. She looks after her husband's parents, an old king who has lost his sight and his kingdom, and his wife. She is gentle with everyone. And through all of it, the epic says, Narada's words stay in her mind, day and night. She is counting. Now, what she doesn't do. She doesn't tell Satyavan or his parents. When the day draws near and she takes a hard vow, fasting and standing through three nights, her father-in-law worries it's too much for her. She doesn't explain; she tells him gently that she will finish it. On the last morning, when Satyavan picks up his axe for the forest, she asks to go along. He's surprised. She asks his parents' leave, and they give it. Nobody hears a lie from her, and nobody hears the reason. Here the epic goes quiet: it never tells us why she keeps the secret. Some readers hear mercy, sparing the people she loves a year of dread. Some hear resolve: telling would turn her vow into everyone's grief. Some just notice how heavy it must have been. The text leaves room for all of them. What it does show is that her silence isn't hiding from the truth. She looks at it every day, counts toward it, and gets ready for it with her own body. A secret can be a way of running. Hers is a way of staying awake.

1344.title: Savitri
1344.hook: Savitri has no weapon and no army on the road behind Death, only a conversation
1344.howItsDone: Hindus hear Savitri's words to Yama when her story is read or retold, in the Mahabharata's forest book, at home, in temple talks, and on the day of the vow some married women keep in her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri in the hermitage, carrying Narada's warning alone and counting the days.

No sword. No army. No spell. When Yama, the lord of death, draws Satyavan's life out of his body and turns south, Savitri has nothing to fight with. What she has is a voice. She walks behind Death and talks, and again and again, Death stops to listen. Last year we followed the boons one by one. Today we listen to what she actually says, because that's what moves him.
screen: `NO SWORD, NO ARMY.` → `SHE WALKS AND TALKS.` → `DEATH STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Yama tells her to turn back. Her first answer is about where she belongs: where her husband is taken, she goes. Then she speaks of friendship. The wise say, she tells him, that walking seven steps together makes people friends, and she has walked more than that beside him. So, as a friend, let him hear her. She doesn't plead with Death as an enemy. She claims him as a companion on the road. Then she speaks of dharma, the right way, and of the good, the people who keep to it. Yama is pleased and offers a gift, anything but Satyavan's life. She asks for her father-in-law's sight. She keeps talking: being near the good, even for a moment, is never wasted. Another gift: her father-in-law's kingdom. The good are kind even to those who wrong them, she says. Another gift: sons for her own father. And the good, she says, hold the world up by their truth. Each time Yama is pleased, and what pleases him is not grief and not cleverness. It's what she says about goodness. Some retellings make it a story of Savitri outwitting Death. The epic tells it more like a conversation Death enjoys. She praises the good to the one who judges everyone, and she means it. This is a week's end, so look back. The week opened with Kunti, then three days with Gandhari: an honest blessing, a folded cloth, a night by the river. Then three with Savitri: her name, her silence, and now her voice. Three women, each holding on with what she had.
screen: `SEVEN STEPS MAKE A FRIEND` · `THE GOOD, AND BEING NEAR THEM` · `KIND EVEN TO THOSE WHO WRONG THEM` · `A CONVERSATION DEATH ENJOYS`
